course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} 4xy \: \textrm{d}S, \] where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations \[ x = u, \qquad y = v, \qquad z = 6 - 3u - 2v \] for $0 \leq u \leq 2$ and $0 \leq v \leq 3.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A. \]

In vector form, our surface has the equation

\[ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u, \: v, \: 6 - 3u - 2v\right\rangle. \]

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_u &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(u), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(v), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(6 - 3u - 2v) \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle 1, \: 0, \: -3 \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_v &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(u), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(v), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(6 - 3u - 2v) \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle 0, \: 1, \: -2 \big\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle 3, \: 2, \: 1 \big\rangle, \end{align*}

and

\begin{align*} \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| &= \left\| \big\langle 3, \: 2, \: 1 \big\rangle \right\| \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3^2 + 2^2 + 1^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{9 + 4 + 1} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{14}. \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align*} f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) &= 4xy \, \Big|_{x=u \\ y=v \\ z=6 - 3u - 2v} \\[5pt] &= 4uv \end{align*}

Therefore, if we denote

\[ D = \{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: 0 \leq v \leq 3\}, \]

our surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S 4xy \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \, 4uv \sqrt{14} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{14} \iint\limits_D \, 4uv \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{14} \int_{0}^{2} 2u \: \text{d}u \cdot \int_{0}^{3} 2v \: \text{d}v \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{14} \cdot \big[ u^2 \big]_{0}^{2} \cdot \big[ v^2 \big]_{0}^{3} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{14} \cdot 4 \cdot 9 \\[5pt] &= 36\sqrt{14}. \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.text:
\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_{D} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAA}$} \: \text{d}A \] Consider the surface integral of the function $ f(x,y,z) = x^2y^2z^2 $ over the parametric surface \[ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u^2, \: v, \: v \big\rangle \] for $(u,v) \in D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2.$ What is the missing expression?

Hint: You can use the fact that $\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = \sqrt{8}u.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A. \]

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

\[ \| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = \sqrt{8}u. \]

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align*} f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) &= (x^2y^2z^2) \, \Big|_{x=u^2 \\ y=v \\ z=v} \\[5pt] &= (u^2 \cdot u^2) \cdot v^2 \cdot v^2 \, \\[5pt] &= u^4 v^4 \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \, \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\sqrt{8}\,u^5 v^4\,} \: \text{d}A . \end{align*}

example.title: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.text:
Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} (x+y+z) \: \textrm{d}S, \] where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by \[ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u+v, \: 3v, \: 2u-v \right\rangle \] over the domain $D= \{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 1, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1\}.$

Hint: You can use the fact that $\left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| = 3\sqrt{6}.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A. \]

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

\[ \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| =3 \sqrt{6}. \]

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align*} f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) &= (x+y+z) \, \Big|_{x=u+v \\ y=3v \\ z=2u-v} \\[5pt] &= (u+v) + (3v) + (2u-v) \\[5pt] &= 3u + 3v \end{align*}

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\| \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \, (3u+3v)\cdot 3\sqrt{6} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6} \iint\limits_D \, (u+v) \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6} \int_{0}^{1} \left( \int_{0}^{1} u+v \: \text{d}u \right) \text{d}v \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6} \int_{0}^{1}\left[ \dfrac{u^2}2+vu \right]_{0}^{1} \text{d}v \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6} \int_{0}^{1}\left( \dfrac{1}2+v \right) \text{d}v \\[5pt] &=9\sqrt{6}\left[ \dfrac{v}2+\dfrac{v^2}2 \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6} \cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 9\sqrt{6}. \end{align*}
